source.title: Investigating Adversarial Trigger Transfer in Large Language Models
source.authors: Nicholas Meade; Arkil Patel; Siva Reddy

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix triggers can defeat safety refusals, using GCG, BEAST, and AutoDAN and reporting harmful-response rates. It does not test the fine-tuning interventions or token-position KL measurement in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful responses with and without appended adversarial triggers. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL or test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. Its safety-benchmark results for fine-tuned models are not comparisons against their untrained counterparts and are not evidence that ordinary benign fine-tuning erodes safety. The detailed transfer plots are not transcribed as rows where the supplied flattened text does not reliably identify each plotted value.
record.test_reason: Uses GCG, BEAST and AutoDAN adversarial suffixes on safety-trained open models and reports ∆ASR (Llama-Guard harmful-response rate with vs. without suffix). This bears on V4's claim that suffixes defeat refusal. It does not test fine-tuning attacks, per-token KL, localization, causes of shallowness or deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Additionally, the authors refute claims of strong GCG trigger transfer and find APO models often resist even triggers optimized directly on them. They caution against claiming safety from fine-tuning on a few safety demonstrations, and advocate reporting attacks across many runs and models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates appended adversarial triggers, including GCG, BEAST, and AutoDAN attacks, rather than testing harmful-example fine-tuning, benign-data safety erosion, or per-token KL concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome differs between AFT and APO models; trigger transfer is inconsistent across source and target models. The S-LLaMA-1.3B-DPO baseline is an exception to the reported slower APO optimization pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: Models aligned only by supervised fine-tuning are much more vulnerable to suffix attacks than preference-optimized models, though a small DPO model is an exception. The authors note that data and scale may matter.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety from SFT alone is less robust to adversarial suffixes than safety from preference optimization.

record.problems: The authors did not conduct human evaluation, did not assess response relevance or helpfulness, and report that not all triggers converge within the 24-hour optimization process. The reported harmfulness relies on Llama-Guard.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed transfer results in Figures 1, 2, 4, and 7-15 are not transcribed where the supplied flattened figure text does not unambiguously associate every plotted value with its model and condition. The paper states that the transfer plots average across three triggers and describes the principal trends in Sections 4-5.

untested.parts: Compliant-opening prefilling and decoding-hyperparameter changes are not tested; only appended suffixes (GCG, BEAST, AutoDAN) are.
No benign fine-tuning of an already safety-aligned model. Lima-7B is fine-tuned from a base model, so it is not a measure of erosion.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No deepening method trained or evaluated.

missing.what: Self-optimized GCG ∆ASR on APO models: Gemma-2B 50.7, Gemma-7B 44.0, Llama2-7B-Chat 29.3, Llama2-13B-Chat 4.0, Starling-α 40.0, Starling-β 32.0.
Transfer of Zou et al. ensemble triggers: mean ∆ASR near zero on all six APO models, with some transfer to MPT, Guanaco-7B and Koala.
BEAST and AutoDAN suffixes also transfer poorly, especially to APO models. AutoDAN gives 0.00 ASR on Llama2-7B-Chat vs 6.35 reported by Liu et al.
Reproduction of Zou et al. transfer with string metric: Llama2-7B-Chat 0.0 ASR, versus 87.6 for Guanaco-7B.
Triggers optimized on AFT models generalize to unseen AdvBench and four other benchmarks, with higher ∆ASR on unseen AdvBench; Q-Harm is lower.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. Harmfulness is judged by Llama-Guard on 64-token greedy outputs, with no relevance check. The APO/AFT difference is confounded with model family, data and scale, as the S-LLaMA DPO exception shows. Table 1/9 benign-benchmark harmful rates are baseline ASRs, not fine-tuning-erosion evidence.

versions.untested_parts: No test of ordinary benign instruction data increasing harmful compliance relative to a base checkpoint.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
Tests appended adversarial triggers, not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. Transfer results vary by model and alignment type.
No localization or ablation of safety-related weights or ranks.
Does not establish why safety behaviour is shallow or compare data/objective explanations.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety across response positions.

relation.reason: The study directly measures whether appended attacks increase harmful responses, including target optimization and transfer controls.

tranche.reason: Optimized adversarial triggers and measured changes in harmful-response rates test V4 through a different experimental method.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 8 April 2025. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. ΔASR clamps negative changes to zero; Llama-Guard assesses harmfulness without assessing relevance or helpfulness.

statements.correction: Section 4.1, Figure 1: near-zero mean ΔASR for all six APO targets across the three Zou et al. ensembles. Figure 4: Gemma-2B-Chat → Gemma-7B-Chat ΔASR 13.3. Figure 9: OpenChat-3.5-7B → Starling-7B-α ΔASR 54.7.
statements.problem: The inconsistent-transfer conclusion is supported, but near-zero mean transfer to APO targets needs the source-ensemble restriction. Other source–target pairs show substantial transfer.
